draft.title: Defences to criminal charges
card: A defence is an argument that an accused person should not be convicted of the crime charged, even if they did the act. The prosecution must still disprove a defence that is raised properly.
if it succeeds, the accused is acquitted, which means found not guilty. Self-defence and duress are examples.
if it succeeds, it does not lead to acquittal. It reduces a charge of murder to manslaughter. Substantial impairment by abnormality of mind is an example.
Self-defence is using reasonable force to protect yourself or another person. Duress is committing an offence because of a threat of serious harm.
draft.remember: A complete defence ends in acquittal. A partial defence still leaves a conviction for manslaughter.

a.q: A jury accepts a partial defence on a murder charge. What is the result?
opts: The accused is convicted of manslaughter instead
The accused is acquitted of all charges
The accused is convicted of murder with a lighter penalty
The trial is stopped and the charge is dropped
a.why: A partial defence reduces murder to manslaughter, so the accused is still convicted of a crime. It does not lead to acquittal, which only a complete defence does.
a.clue: Partial means the accused is not fully cleared.

b.q: Sam is charged with assault. He says a gang threatened to seriously harm his family unless he hit a shop worker. If the jury accepts this defence, what is the outcome?
opts: Acquittal, because duress is a complete defence
Conviction for manslaughter, as a partial defence
Conviction for assault, with a reduced charge
Acquittal, because the prosecution dropped the case
b.why: Sam claims he acted because of a threat of serious harm, which is duress. Duress is a complete defence, so if it succeeds he is acquitted. It is not partial: reducing murder to manslaughter does not apply, as this is not a murder charge.
b.clue: Name the defence from the threat, then decide if it is complete.

a.best: The accused is convicted of manslaughter instead

b.best: Acquittal, because duress is a complete defence

problems.detail: The card says the prosecution must disprove any defence that is properly raised, then gives substantial impairment as its example of a partial defence. In NSW, the accused must prove substantial impairment on the balance of probabilities (Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) s 23A(4)). The prosecution-disproves rule holds for self-defence and duress, but not for this defence.

The line on who must disprove a defence teaches burden-of-proof content, which belongs to point 2 (The burden and standard of proof). It should be mentioned only, or removed, rather than explained here.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The card wrongly implies the prosecution must disprove every defence, including substantial impairment, where the accused carries the burden in NSW. That burden-of-proof line also strays into point 2.
